plan: SAT R&W batch 66: 8 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000592..000599 (Herculaneum scrolls WIC, Venus flytrap inference, seed-soaking quantitative evidence, Nazca lines cross-text (Reiche/Hawkins), Katherine Johnson purpose, Terracotta Army agreement, Gwendolyn Brooks boundary, Mae Jemison transition). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S065-09 (Nobel nomination rule) and S065-11 (importation wording) resubmitted with factual corrections on their previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Reading without unrolling
passages.text: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, it buried a library of papyrus scrolls in the town of Herculaneum and turned them to charcoal. The carbonized scrolls are so ______ that past attempts to unroll them by hand often reduced them to fragments. In 2023, researchers instead used X-ray scans and computer analysis to read words from inside a scroll that had never been opened.

passages.title: Counting touches
passages.text: The leaves of a Venus flytrap close around prey only after trigger hairs on their surface are touched twice within about twenty to thirty seconds. A single touch does not shut the trap. Researchers have also found that the plant begins producing digestive enzymes only after the trigger hairs have been touched several more times. The two-touch requirement likely helps the plant avoid ______

passages.title: Soaking seeds
passages.text:
A student soaked bean seeds in water for different lengths of time before planting and recorded the percent that germinated.
No soaking: 40%
6 hours: 62%
12 hours: 78%
24 hours: 77%
The student claims that soaking longer than 12 hours provided no additional benefit.

passages.title: Lines in the desert
passages.text:
Text 1
In the mid-twentieth century, the German mathematician Maria Reiche spent decades studying the Nazca lines, huge figures and long straight lines scratched into the desert of southern Peru. She argued that many of the lines pointed to the rising and setting positions of the Sun and stars and served as an astronomical calendar.

Text 2
In 1968, the astronomer Gerald Hawkins tested this idea by comparing the directions of many lines with the positions of astronomical events. He found that the lines matched such events no more often than lines pointing in random directions would. Later researchers have proposed that the lines were paths walked in rituals, some possibly connected to water.

passages.title: Checking the machine
passages.text: Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at NASA whose calculations helped plan the paths of early American spaceflights. By 1962, NASA had begun using electronic computers to calculate orbits, but many astronauts did not yet fully trust them. Before his orbital flight that year, John Glenn asked that Johnson check the computer's results by hand. Her calculations matched, and the flight went ahead.

passages.title: An army of clay
passages.text: Discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, the Terracotta Army, made to guard the tomb of the first emperor of China, ______ of thousands of life-size clay soldiers, each with an individually shaped face.

passages.title: A first prize
passages.text: In 1950, Gwendolyn Brooks became the first Black author to win a Pulitzer ______ she received the award for Annie Allen, a collection of poems about a girl growing up in Chicago.

passages.title: Many fields
passages.text: Mae Jemison became the first African American woman to travel into space when she flew aboard the space shuttle Endeavour in 1992. Her interests, however, were never limited to spaceflight. Before joining NASA, she served as a Peace Corps medical officer in Sierra Leone and Liberia. ______ after leaving NASA in 1993, she founded a technology company and taught environmental studies at Dartmouth College.

passages.title: Notes on an image
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1952, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made an X-ray image of DNA known as Photo 51.
- In 1953, Maurice Wilkins showed the image to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge.
- Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix model of DNA later in 1953.
- Franklin died in 1958.
- The 1962 Nobel Prize for the structure of DNA went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
- Under the Nobel rules of the time, a person who had died could not be nominated, and Franklin had never been nominated.

passages.title: Notes on a ship
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Clotilda was the last known ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States, arriving in Alabama in 1860, decades after bringing enslaved people into the country was outlawed.
- After the voyage, the ship was burned to hide evidence of the crime.
- Many of the people it carried later founded Africatown, a community near Mobile.
- Descendants of those people still live in Africatown.
- In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.explanation: Scrolls that fall to pieces when handled are "brittle."

A.rationale: Their value would not explain why unrolling them broke them apart.

B.rationale: Age alone does not explain why the scrolls fell apart when unrolled.

D.rationale: The text says the scrolls were hard to read without being destroyed.

hints: What happened when people tried to unroll them?
candidates.remember: Use the result described after the blank to define it.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: closing on raindrops or debris that touch it only once.
choices.B: being eaten by animals that feed on its leaves.
choices.C: producing digestive enzymes before the trap has closed.
choices.D: catching insects that are too small to digest.

candidates.evidence: A single touch does not shut the trap
candidates.explanation: Requiring two touches in a short time means a single accidental contact, such as a raindrop, will not trigger a costly closure.

B.rationale: The text says nothing about animals eating the plant.

C.rationale: Enzyme production depends on later touches, not on the two-touch rule for closing.

D.rationale: The text does not discuss prey size.

hints: What kinds of things might touch a leaf only once?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the rule filters out.

candidates.remember: An inference should follow from the mechanism described.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Germination rose from 40% with no soaking to 62% after 6 hours of soaking.
choices.B: Germination was 78% after 12 hours of soaking and 77% after 24 hours.
choices.C: Germination was highest, 78%, after 12 hours of soaking.
choices.D: Every soaking time produced higher germination than no soaking.

candidates.evidence: soaking longer than 12 hours provided no additional benefit
candidates.explanation: Comparing 12 hours (78%) with 24 hours (77%) shows that longer soaking added nothing.

A.rationale: This shows a benefit of short soaking, not the lack of benefit after 12 hours.

C.rationale: This gives one value but does not compare 12 hours with longer soaking.

D.rationale: This is true but does not address soaking beyond 12 hours.

hints: Which two values test the claim?

strategy.explanation: Find the data on both sides of 12 hours.

candidates.remember: Support a claim with the data it is about.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Hawkins (Text 2) most likely respond to Reiche's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: He would agree that the lines were a calendar but say they tracked only the Sun.
choices.B: He would argue that the lines were created much later than Reiche believed.
choices.C: He would claim that the lines were definitely paths connected to water.
choices.D: He would say the lines match such events no more often than chance predicts.

candidates.evidence: no more often than lines pointing in random directions would
candidates.explanation: Hawkins tested the calendar idea and found the alignments were no more frequent than chance, which undercuts Reiche's argument.

A.rationale: Hawkins found no meaningful alignment with any astronomical events.

B.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about when the lines were made.

C.rationale: Text 2 attributes the ritual-path idea to later researchers and calls the water link possible.

strategy.explanation: Compare Hawkins's finding with Reiche's claim.

candidates.remember: Identify whether a second text supports or undermines the first.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To show how one mathematician's work helped build trust in new computing methods
choices.B: To argue that electronic computers were less accurate than human mathematicians
choices.C: To explain how NASA calculated the orbits of early spacecraft
choices.D: To describe the events of John Glenn's orbital flight in detail

candidates.evidence: Her calculations matched, and the flight went ahead
candidates.explanation: The text introduces Johnson, explains astronauts' distrust of computers, and shows how her matching hand calculations allowed the flight to proceed.

B.rationale: The text says Johnson's calculations matched the computer's.

C.rationale: The text does not explain the methods of calculation.

D.rationale: The flight itself is mentioned only briefly at the end.

hints: Why does the text mention Glenn's request?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The subject "the Terracotta Army" is singular; the phrases around it do not change that, so the verb is "consists."

A.rationale: "Consist" is plural, but the subject "Terracotta Army" is singular.

C.rationale: "Consisting" is not a finite verb, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

D.rationale: "To consist" is not a finite verb, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

hints: What is the subject of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Skip the descriptive phrases to find the verb's subject.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite verb that agrees with its subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: she received the award for Annie Allen
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, so a semicolon correctly joins them.

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: "Which she received the award for" creates an ungrammatical clause.

strategy.explanation: Find where the first clause ends.

candidates.remember: Join independent clauses with a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a conjunction.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Her interests, however, were never limited to spaceflight
candidates.explanation: Both her service before NASA and her work after it illustrate interests beyond spaceflight, so an additive transition fits.

A.rationale: Her work after NASA continues, rather than contrasts with, the breadth shown before NASA.

B.rationale: Her Peace Corps service did not cause her later work.

D.rationale: Her later work did not replace her earlier service.

hints: What do the two examples have in common?

strategy.explanation: Find the claim both examples support.

candidates.remember: Use "likewise" to add a parallel example.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why Franklin did not share the 1962 Nobel Prize. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 1952, Franklin and Raymond Gosling made Photo 51, an X-ray image of DNA.
choices.B: Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson in 1953 without Franklin's knowledge.
choices.C: The 1962 Nobel Prize for DNA's structure went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
choices.D: Franklin had died in 1958, and people who had died could not be nominated.

candidates.evidence: a person who had died could not be nominated
candidates.explanation: Only choice D connects Franklin's death in 1958 with the rule that a person who had died could not be nominated, which explains why she was not among the 1962 winners.

A.rationale: This describes her work but does not explain the prize outcome.

B.rationale: This describes how the image was used, not why she did not share the prize.

C.rationale: This states who won but not why Franklin was not included.

strategy.explanation: Find the notes that give a reason.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

revision_history.reason: both solvers: "Nobel Prizes are not awarded after death" oversimplified the rule as of 1962
revision_history.change: note and key reworded to the nomination rule; Franklin never nominated

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (emphasizing significance to a community)
candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the 2019 discovery mattered to Africatown's residents. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda, which had been burned in 1860.
choices.B: For Africatown residents, including descendants of the ship's captives, the discovery confirmed a hidden history.
choices.C: The Clotilda arrived in Alabama in 1860, decades after importing enslaved people into the United States was outlawed.
choices.D: Africatown, a community near Mobile, Alabama, was founded by people who had been brought to the United States.

candidates.evidence: Descendants of those people still live in Africatown
candidates.explanation: Only choice B links the discovery to the residents, many of whom descend from the people the ship carried.

A.rationale: This states the discovery but not why it mattered to Africatown.

C.rationale: This gives background but does not mention the residents or the discovery.

D.rationale: This describes the community but not the discovery.

hints: Which choice connects the discovery to the residents?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the exact goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must address the goal's specific focus.

revision_history.reason: both blind solvers: "its captives" had no clear antecedent; "many descended" overstated the notes
revision_history.change: key reworded to "including descendants of the ship's captives"

revision_history.reason: blind solver: "the trade was outlawed" overstated; only importation was banned (1808)
revision_history.change: note and choice C reworded to importation
